## Mutations
The MOVICS package provides a function ``compMut()`` which applies independent testing (i.e., Fisher' s exact test or $\chi^2$ test) for each mutation, and generates a table with statistical results and creates an OncoPrint using those differentially mutated genes. Here we use the $p$-value simulation method,because Fisher's exact test was computationally intense for the 9 clusters.

<b>Oncoprint:</b>

## Differential Analysis
DGEA is performed in order to compare the expression of the two identified consensus subtypes using the __limma__ package.

In order to identify subtype-specific markers, we find the markers that are up-regulated in `r paste0(params$algorithm, 1)` vs. all other clusters and the ones which are down-regulated in `r paste0(params$algorithm, 1)` vs. all other clusters etc.

In this procedure, the most differentially expressed genes sorted by __log2FoldChange__ are chosen as the biomarkers for each subtype (200 biomarkers for each subtype by default; Here we set 200 -> 100 markers). These biomarkers should pass the significance threshold (e.g., nominal $p$-value < 0.05 and adjusted $p$-value < 0.05) and must not overlap with any biomarkers identified for other subtypes.

<b>Up-regulated gene expression markers</b>
![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/NEMO/pdf2png/upregulated_biomarkers_heatmap_using_upregulated_genes-1.png")`)

## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis

GSEA is carried out using a gene set background which includes all gene sets derived from GO biological processes (``Resources/Pathways/c5.go.bp.v2024.1.Hs.symbols.gmt``) from The Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB, https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/index.jsp).

Likewise, these identified specific pathways should pass the significance threshold (e.g., nominal $p$-value < 0.05 and adjusted $p$-value < 0.25; we set the latter to <u>0.1</u>) and must not overlap with any pathways identified for other subtypes. After having the subtype-specific pathways, genes that are inside the pathways are retrieved to calculate a single sample enrichment score by using ``GSVA`` R package. Subsequently, subtype-specific enrichment score will be represented by the mean or median (mean by default) value within the subtype, and will be further visualized by diagonal heatmap.

![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/NEMO/pdf2png/upregulated_pathway_heatmap_using_upregulated_pathways-1.png")`)

MOVICS provides a simple function which uses gene set variation analysis to calculate an enrichment score for each sample in each subtype based on given gene set list of interest.

# Evaluation results
## Nearest Template Prediction (NTP)
MOVICS provides two model-free approaches for subtype prediction in validation cohort. First, MOVICS switches to nearest template prediction ([NTP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21124904/)) which can be flexibly applied to cross-platform, cross-species, and multiclass predictions without any optimization of analysis parameters.

Here cosine similarity is used to compare external samples to class templates (here we use the up-regulated genes in the form of a binary matrix with columns: "cluster #" where an entry is 1 if the gene is up-regulated in the cluster # or -1 otherwise). The nearest class for each sample is determined by the smallest distance (converted from cosine similarity here). Each sample's result includes the nearest class prediction, the distance to all templates, and the p-value of the prediction.

The function randomly permutes the sample labels multiple times (here ``nPerm = 10000``) to generate a null distribution of similarity scores between samples and class templates. For each observed sample-to-template distance, the function compares it against the null distribution to calculate a $p$-value. This $p$-value indicates the likelihood that the observed match could have occurred by chance. The $p$-values are adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) method to control for multiple hypothesis testing, ensuring robust statistical inference.

![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/NEMO/pdf2png/ntp_expr_up_heatmap_transNEO-1.png")`)
![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/NEMO/pdf2png/ntp_expr_down_heatmap_transNEO-1.png")`)

Results on the comparisons of `r params$evaluation_source` clinical variables with respect to the predicted consensus subtypes are summarised in [this file](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/NEMO/transNEO_Summary_of_clinical_variables.txt")`).

<b>Exact test results by MOVICS:</b>

## Partition Around Medoids (PAM)

To be specific, ``runPAM()`` first trains a partition around medoids (PAM) classifier in the discovery (training) cohort (i.e., `r params$data_source`) to predict the subtype for patients in the external validation (testing) cohort (i.e., `r params$evaluation_source`), and each sample in the validation cohort was assigned to a subtype label whose centroid had the highest Pearson correlation with the sample. Finally, the [in-group proportion (IGP)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16613834/) statistic (the proportion of samples within a cluster that were classified into the same cluster upon random permutation of the data) is estimated to evaluate the similarity and reproducibility of the acquired subtypes between discovery and validation cohorts (i.e. are the clusters identified in `r params$data_source` reproducible in `r params$evaluation_source` after label permutation).

<u>Compare NEMO `r params$data_source` vs. PAM `r params$data_source`:</u>

## Subtype agreement
Here we examine how similar the consensus multi-omic clustering labels are to other labels relative to breast cancer.

MOVICS provides function of ``compAgree()`` to calculate four statistics: Rand Index (RI), Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI), Jaccard Index (JI), and Fowlkes-Mallows (FM); all these measurements range from 0 to 1 and the larger the value is, the more similar the compared groups are. 

![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/NEMO/pdf2png/Classification_agreement-1.png")`)

## Comparison to MOVICS NEMO

In MOVICS, the NEMO algorithm is run by default with $nn = \frac{n}{6}$ and $\sigma = 0.5$.

<b>ARI:</b> `r params$ARI_to_MOVICS_NEMO`
<b>NMI:</b> `r params$NMI_to_MOVICS_NEMO`

# Conclusions
<ol>
  <li>NEMO identifies `r params$hyperparameters$eigengap_k` subtypes in the data.</li>
  <li>The identified NEMO subtypes are associated with <b>race, PR status, ER status, HER2 status, no. of lymph nodes positive (by H&E), ER and PR cell level percentages</b>, as determined by statistical tests in ``MOVICS::compClinvar()``.</li>
  <li>The identified NEMO subtypes are not particularly similar to the MOVICS NEMO subtypes (<b>ARI:</b> `r params$ARI_to_MOVICS_NEMO`, <b>NMI:</b> `r params$NMI_to_MOVICS_NEMO`).</li>
  <li>When looking at the <b>comprehensive multi-omic heatmap</b>, we observe noticeable omic patterns for some of the NEMO subtypes:
    <ul>
      <li><b>Subtypes 1 and 3 are predominantly ER+</b> and have similar expression and methylation profiles, but different CNV profiles.</li>
      <li><b>Subtype 2 is predominantly ER-</b> and has different expression, CNV and methylation profiles than most other subtypes.</li>
      <li>Subtype 5 has a distinctly different expression and methylation profile than the rest of the subtypes, relatively similar to Subtype 2. That may be due to the roughly equal distribution of ER+ and ER- in this subtype.</li>
      <li><b>Subtype 9 is heavily mutated</b> compared to all other subtypes.</li>
    </ul>
  <li>Based on the dimensionality reduction plots of the original matrices, a clearer separation of samples is noticed on the <b>methylation, miRNA and SNPs modalities</b>.</li>
  <li>Although NEMO1 and NEMO3 are both predominantly ER+, NEMO1 has the majority of <b>ILC samples</b> and a noticeably lower percentage of <em>TP53</em> mutations (<b>NEMO1:</b> 8.4%, <b>NEMO2</b>: 20.8%). Roughly <b>50%</b> of NEMO1 samples have mutations in <em>PIK3CA</em>, compared to only <b>12.5%</b> in NEMO3.</li>
  <li>NEMO2 has a high percentage of <em>TP53</em> mutations (71.7%).</li>
  <li>NEMO8 and NEMO9 are heavily mutated (although small in sample size: 32 and 39 respectively) compared to the rest of the subtypes in most of the identified significant genes:
    <ul>
      <li>NEMO9 has a percentage of mutated samples higher than **12%** for all identified genes. The highest proportions are observed in <em>TTN</em> (**60.5%**), <em><PIK3CA</em> (**50.0%**) and <em>MUC16</em> (**44.7%**).</li>
      <li>NEMO8 is not as hevily burdened, but has high proportions of mutated samples in <em>TP53</em> (**53.1%**), <em>TTN</em> (**43.8%**) and <em>PIK3CA</em> (**40.6%**).</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>According to the **naïve FGA plots**, __the gain patterns are significantly different across NEMO subtypes__, while according to the more conservative **COSMIC FGA plots**, __the loss patterns are significantly different across NEMO subtypes__. Both FGA plots agree on **significant differences across subtypes regarding overall FGA**.</li>
  <li>In terms of pathways:
    <ul>
      <li>NEMO1 has up-regulated **extracellular component pathways**, **microtubule bundle formation pathways** and **axoneme pathways** compared to all other subtypes.</li>
      <li>NEMO2 has up-regulated **nucleotide synthesis and metabolism pathways** as well as **cell division pathways** (see corresponding [file](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/NEMO/_dgea__limma_test_result.NEMO2_unique_upexpr_pathway.txt")`) as well).</li>
      <li>NEMO3 demonstrates increased **cytokinesis** and **ubiquitin-dependent pathways**.</li>
      <li>NEMO5 is associated with **negative regulation of VEGF** and **miRNA-mediated gene silencing by inhibition of translation**.</li>
      <li>NEMO9 is associated with **increased immune activity**.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>NEMO3 has generally <b>lower immune system activity</b> compared to all other subtypes.</li>
  <li>Overall, NEMO subtypes exhibit high agremeent scores with ER status as seen in the **Subtype Agreement plot**.</li>
  <li>Predicted NEMO subtypes on the transNEO cohort are associated with ER status, HER2 status grade, <b>pCR</b> (see table below), PAM50, iC10, type of regimen of neoadjuvant treatment, RCB score, STAT1.gsva score, GGI.gsva score, ESC.gsva score, TMB and HRD.sum. </li>
</ol>

```{r resp_table, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# Create the data frame
table_data <- table(params$transNEO_var2comp[[params$algorithm]], params$transNEO_var2comp[[params$algorithm]])

# Calculate percentages
percentage_data <- 100 * prop.table(table_data, 1)

# Create a function to format the output as "count (percentage%)"
format_response <- function(counts, percentages) {
  paste0(counts, " (", round(percentages, 1), "%)")
}

# Initialize an empty data frame
data_resp <- data.frame(Response = c("pCR", "Residual Disease"))

# Loop over the groups to fill the data frame
for (alg_group in rownames(table_data)) {
  pcr_counts <- table_data[alg_group, "pCR"]
  rd_counts <- table_data[alg_group, "Residual Disease"]
  
  pcr_percent <- percentage_data[alg_group, "pCR"]
  rd_percent <- percentage_data[alg_group, "Residual Disease"]
  
  # Add the formatted values to the data frame
  data_resp[[alg_group]] <- c(
    format_response(pcr_counts, pcr_percent),
    format_response(rd_counts, rd_percent)
  )
}

# Print the table using knitr::kable
knitr::kable(data_resp, caption = paste0("Response rates across transNEO", params$algorithm, " subtypes"))
```
